parts:
I attempted the proof — and it succeeded, but in a way that turns out to be the most useful possible outcome for the program: **Conjecture 6.1 as literally stated is a theorem, unconditionally**, and the proof exposes a loophole in the statement itself. The 13-page note delivered above (`second_involution_resolution.tex/.pdf`) contains the full treatment.

The short version: because the conjecture says "for every $c$ *there are points* $Z(c_1,\lambda_1),\dots$", the sample points may be chosen *after* $c$ — with knowledge of the answer. I proved a **uniform oscillation lemma** (the honest math in the note): $F(c) = \operatorname{Re} Z(c,\log 2)$ is real-analytic and has oscillation $\geq r > 0$ on every window, via the Guinand–Weil decomposition into a slowly-varying archimedean part plus a Bohr almost-periodic prime part with $B_2 = 0.5407 \neq 0$ at frequency $\log 2$. Given that, the intermediate value theorem lets you *encode* $D(c)$ into the difference $F(c_1) - F(c_2)$ of two adaptively chosen samples, and one fixed Möbius-type semialgebraic $S$ decodes it — so the conjecture holds with $N=2$, $\Lambda(\varepsilon) = \log 2$ independent of $\varepsilon$, and error exactly $0$. That over-fulfillment is the tell: the mechanism consumes no arithmetic (it computes the defect of Euler-product-free multisets identically — demonstrated numerically by recovering $D = 0.125$ to $10^{-15}$ on a synthetic multiset with an off-line quadruple), so it passes your own hardness checks vacuously. The selection map is an infinite-capacity side channel.

The note then does the constructive work: a **repaired non-adaptive conjecture** (fixed offsets, translation-covariant sampling), a **class-uniform version** over an axiomatized explicit-formula class (with the observation that DH is *not* in that class — and that whether the class contains off-line members is itself a Weil-positivity-type question), the **shifted family $\Xi_\alpha = \Xi(z+i\alpha)\Xi(z-i\alpha)$** as a testbed with known nonzero defect and an exact reduction to $\zeta$, and a **lower bound theorem**: non-adaptive continuous semialgebraic estimators at scale $\Lambda$ can't resolve an isolated defect at height $x_0$ unless $\Lambda \geq (1-o(1))\log\log x_0$ — the first entry in the "matching lower bound" genre your Question 6.2 asks for, proved by Kronecker near-recurrence of finite-scale data.

Everything was adversarially reviewed by two independent agents: all core results and constants were reproduced from scratch; they caught real errors in my first version of the lower-bound proof (a truncation-tail bound and a misstated Dirichlet claim) plus a DH overclaim — all fixed in the delivered version. Numerics are fully certified (`lab_run_si_check.py`, ALL PASS): explicit formula to $10^{-14}$, oscillation $\geq 2.01$ on all windows up to height $10^6$. The note, both lab scripts, and an updated `paper_STATUS.md` (with action items, including the decision of which repaired form to put into the intro paper) are saved to the project.

One caveat to keep in view: Theorem 5.3 constrains continuous estimators only, and the DH oscillation is verified numerically-by-analogy, not proved — both are flagged honestly in Remark 5.4 of the note.

Done — the memo version is delivered above and saved to the project (replacing the earlier draft). What changed: the author block is gone and it's now framed as a research memo ("August 2026 — research memo, unreviewed"); an unnumbered section right after the table of contents tells the story in one paragraph — the program, the AI-assisted drafting, the two independent AI review passes and what they caught, and the explicit statement that it has had no human expert review, which is what circulation is meant to solicit. That section also gives a prospective reviewer a suggested order of scrutiny: the encoding proof first (elementary, and the heart of it), then the oscillation lemma (classical ingredients only), then the model lower bound, flagged honestly as the least polished part.

For the shop-around audience I also made it self-contained: the conjecture is restated in full so nobody needs the companion drafts, which now appear in the bibliography unattributed as "unpublished companion draft, available from the program maintainer on request" — so the memo itself carries no name, and you decide what to share when someone bites. The reproducibility note at the end points to the two lab scripts (both in the project, both passing all checks) so a skeptical reader can rerun the numerics in minutes.

One thought for when you circulate it: the two most self-contained "hooks" for an expert are the oscillation lemma (a clean, checkable, unconditional statement about explicit-formula data) and the sharply posed RH-free open problem in Section 8, item 4 — either could interest someone even if they don't want to engage with the whole program.
